title: Ogre Gannet and the Sunstone Pact
markdown:
Ogre Gannet lived in a snug cottage high in the Whispering Peaks, where the air tasted of pine needles and fresh snow and the loudest sound was usually the wind deciding what to do with a crag. He was not the sort of ogre who practised looming. He charted clouds. His calloused fingers, which could have been for clubs, drew cirrus and storm with a surprising lightness, and the cottage held scrolls of sky instead of bones, plus a serious collection of smooth grey river stones. He liked the sky’s predictable cycles and the weight of a good stick of charcoal.

For decades a low hum of unease had lived under the mountain quiet. It concerned the Sunstone Berry Patch, where the fruit grew plump enough to make a stern goat reconsider its dignity. The trouble was the border. The patch sat on the edge of Gannet’s land and the territory of the Grumbleclaw clan, who were prickly by reputation and by practice. The argument had been inherited so thoroughly that no one remembered the first insult, only the habit of having one. Gannet, who preferred logic to feud, thought it time to settle the thing with dignity: a clear line, a few cairns, a polite exchange. The thought of facing the Grumbleclaws — and of looking clumsy while trying to look sensible — made his whiskers twitch. He packed honey cakes for everyone anyway.

“A new boundary,” he told the empty kitchen, settling his spectacles. “Cairns. Courtesy. Then cirrus.”

The path down was ancient stone and rope bridges over gaps that enjoyed being gaps. He had not walked it in years. At the first bridge the ropes looked tired and the planks offered opinions. Gannet’s chest tightened. He pictured the picnic basket scattering, a public stumble, the exact opposite of dignity. He did not name the feeling. He put a boot on the first plank and felt it argue back.

A metallic clang came from further down. Owain Cogsworth, the wizard surveyor, was bent over parchment, muttering incantations that shimmered in the cold. His staff, Rumble, had developed a loud and editorial voice, and was already frowning at the terrain with the whole of its polished wood.

“Honestly, Owain,” Rumble boomed, gravel in the grain. “These ropes insult their own strength. A gust and we take an unscheduled flight. And that cliff face? Unsuited for a dignified cairn. A marker there would look lost. A teacup on a summit.”

Gannet approached as softly as a large ogre can. He cleared his throat, distant thunder trying to be polite. “Good day, Master Cogsworth. Rumble. I am Gannet. I am here to finish the boundary for the Sunstone Berry Patch. I hope the journey has been agreeable.”

Owain looked up, eyes bright behind spectacles that had slipped. “Ah, Gannet. Splendid. Yes, the patch. Rumble has been vocal about its tricks. He fancies himself an expert on roots and erosion.”

“Complexities,” Gannet said, even, and disliked being outdone by a stick that sounded so finished.

“Indeed,” Rumble declared. “Poorly conceived from the outset. The patch thrives on this particular mash of microclimates. A line drawn by grumpy landowners is an insult to the weather. Like slicing a rainbow. Pointless. Ugly.”

Heat climbed Gannet’s neck. He had measured for weeks. “The Grumbleclaws and I agreed on a division. Respect for the agreement. Order.”

“Respect for a squabble as stale as last year’s snow?” Rumble’s voice sharpened. “The patch needs stewardship, not masters. A voice that understands fruit, not a map.”

They went on, the picnic basket a careful pendulum at Gannet’s side, honey cakes arguing softly with one another. He held his dignity like a cup filled too near the rim. Owain scribbled elevations and wind notes, sometimes smiling at his staff as if the commentary were a billed feature of the survey. Rumble reviewed every loose stone, every whistling gust, the angle of a cairn that did not yet exist, and the frankly questionable structural integrity of certain ancient mountain goats they passed, who looked back as if they had opinions about wizardry.

“That goat,” Rumble said, “is a monument to erosion and stubbornness. Do not take advice from it.”

Gannet, who had not been about to, felt his ears heat anyway.

They reached a narrow ledge that the mountain had not quite finished. Wind howled in a way that copied Gannet’s stomach. The path became a series of moss-slick stones with mist for a neighbour. He saw himself below — mission, cakes, spectacles, the whole dignified project — becoming a story the Grumbleclaws would tell with toothy pleasure. Owain would sigh. Rumble would produce a perfectly cut remark about ogre locomotion. He froze. The basket handle creaked in his fist.

Owain patted his forearm. “Don’t look at the drop. Look at the rock. It has been here a thousand years. It can take you.”

Gannet felt the cool grit under his boot, the damp after-rain smell, the wind at his ears. He stepped. Then again. He did not stumble. Relief arrived without a speech. Rumble, for a wonder, said nothing about locomotion.

The Sunstone Berry Patch was a riot of crimson and green, berries like small suns in the late light. Owain produced a measuring tape of moonlight and spider-silk. Rumble planted itself with a thud that meant veto.

“Stop. You will not divide this. It belongs to the mountain and to anyone hungry enough to be honest. This is a feast, not a deed.”

Gannet looked at Owain, who seemed rather pleased with his staff’s eloquence, and at the Grumbleclaw delegation, arrived in their inherited scowls, which had gone confused around the edges and, in one or two faces, hopeful. The clean line, the cairns, the sensible ending he had sketched on three separate scrolls — all of it was crumbling like a biscuit left in weather. He could insist, force the tape, and restart the feud with a wooden antagonist as the new star. He could walk home with unused cakes and a dignity that had never been tested by fruit.

He felt the weave of his tunic, familiar. He smelled the berries, sweet enough to make a plan look small. Bees worked as if no one had ever drawn a border. The Grumbleclaws eyed the fruit with undisguised longing, claws polite for once. A different dignity offered itself: less line, more table. He imagined the lonely walk if he pushed and lost, gravel underfoot, the scent fading. He imagined, riskier, the silence if he offered something and they laughed. Both futures stood on the same moss.

“Rumble,” Gannet said, steadier than he expected. “Dividing it would be a shame.” He met the Grumbleclaws’ eyes. “What if it were shared? Ogres, Grumbleclaws, the sprites who tiptoe through. And you,” he added, hopeful and a little sly, “could be guardian. Fair. Vocal. No one takes more than a share.”

Murmurs. Curiosity instead of the old grimace. Owain beamed and shoved his spectacles up. Rumble went silent long enough for Gannet to hear his own pulse. Then a thoughtful thrum.

“A guardian. Neutral arbiter of berry distribution. Ecological harmony. Equitable access for sentient beings with a discernible need for fruit.” A pause of leaves. “Well. That sounds rather splendid. I accept.”

So the patch became the peaks’ first communal orchard. A polished stone with a simple swirl marked a boundary that was, in practice, invisible. Rumble stood beside it and issued stern notes on etiquette to anyone whose pockets looked ambitious. Gannet walked home lighter, cakes mostly given away, charcoal waiting.

Weeks later a young Grumbleclaw, freckled and not yet practised at scowling, dropped a ripe berry on the path. It rolled toward a steep edge. Gannet, who had come for a lenticular cloud, watched the boy’s face fall — then turn toward Rumble, who said nothing, which was a kind of permission. The boy found a mossy foothold, snatched the berry, and grinned as if he had invented balance. Gannet grinned back, the cloud forgotten for a minute. Rumble stood tall, polish full of sun, and did not comment on anyone’s feet.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
